sections.text: Rust has two main string types. String is owned text you can grow and change. &str is a borrowed view of some text, like a string literal.

len() counts bytes, not characters. Rust stores text as UTF-8, where a plain English letter takes one byte but a letter like é, or an emoji, takes two to four. To count characters, use chars().count():
Because a character can be more than one byte, Rust won't let you write s[0] to get the first character. Use s.chars() to walk through the characters instead.
Join strings with format!, which is usually clearer than +:

The + operator takes the String on its left by value: it moves it, adds the &str on the right to the end, and hands back the same String. That's why the right side must be a &str (write a + &b when b is a String), and why a can't be used after a + b.
Strings come with many useful methods:

Rust strings are always valid UTF-8. len() is instant because it's stored, while chars().count() has to walk the whole string. Use bytes() for raw bytes and char_indices() when you need character positions that are safe to slice at. A char is a Unicode scalar value, so a letter that looks like one to a reader, such as é typed as e plus an accent, can be several chars; a crate such as unicode-segmentation counts those as one.
A good rule: store text in a String, and take &str when a function only needs to read it.
